complaint.title: Lok Shakti Abhiyan et. al. vs ABP
complaint.subtitle: POSCO’s involvement in HR and environmental impact in India
complainants: Norwegian Forum for Environment and Development
affected: Other NCP's where the complaint was filed
complaint.concluded: 13 March 2013, Related complaints, Lok Shakti Abhiyan et.al vs Norwegian Government Pension Fund – Global, Lok Shakti Abhiyan et al. vs POSCO
complaint.allegations:
The complaint, filed by Lok Shakti Abhiyan and supporting coalitions in S. Korea, Netherlands, and Norway, concerns POSCOs failure to seek to prevent human rights abuses and carry out comprehensive human rights and environmental studies for its proposed iron mine, steel plant and associated infrastructure in the State of Odisha, India.
The complaint alleges POSCOs efforts to construct a 12 million-ton per annum integrated steel plant, captive power plant, captive port and other related infrastructure in the Jagatsinghpur District will lead to the physical and economic displacement of more than 20,000 people, including individuals who have special legal protections under the Scheduled Tribes or Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act. The complainants maintain POSCO has not engaged in meaningful stakeholder consultation with all affected communities to identify the full scope and severity of human rights, social and environmental impacts. The complainants fear that POSCOs failure to conduct due diligence will mean the company will be incapable of preventing or mitigating significant adverse impacts on thousands of people and the environment.
The complaint also addresses the responsibility of the Dutch pension fund ABP and the Norwegian Government Pension Fund  Global (along with the pension funds asset managers APG and NBIM) for investing in POSCO. The complaint calls on the pension funds to seek to prevent or mitigate adverse impacts directly linked to their operations through their financial relationships with POSCO.
complaint.outcome:
The complaint was filed simultaneously at the Korean, Dutch and Norwegian NCPs.
The Dutch NCP, dealing with the case against ABP, accepted the complaint and successfully facilitated several meetings between the parties. In March 2013, a joint final statement was issued in which ABP and APG commit to exercise their leverage bringing POSCOs business practices in line with international standards. The joint statement calls on the three NCPs involved to jointly commission a review and assessment mission to India and to help to facilitate a meaningful stakeholder consultation process.
Following the joint agreement, the Dutch NCP published a statement confirming that the OECD Guidelines apply to minority shareholdings. This sets an important precedent for future cases against financial institutions. The Dutch NCP has offered to assist the Korean NCP in handling its part of the case.
The Norwegian NCP accepted the case and tried to facilitate mediation. However, NBIM refused to engage with the NCP. On 27 May 2013, the Norwegian NCP published its final statement reaffirming the Dutch NCPs assertion that the Guidelines apply to minority shareholders. The NCP further concluded that NBIM was in violation of the OECD Guidelines for refusing to cooperate with the NCP, and for lacking a strategy on how to address human rights risks related to companies in which it invests.
The Korean NCP sent the complaint to POSCO for a response. POSCO denied the allegations, and the NCP requested additional information from the complainants, which they provided. In June 2013 the NCP rejected the complaint as it determined it could not play a role in resolving the dispute, which they consider to be the responsibility of the Indian authorities.
In response to the request of the Dutch parties in their statement, the Dutch NCP explored the possibility of jointly organising a mission to India by the three NCPs involved. However, the Norwegian and South Korean NCPs were unwilling to participate, as they consider the case to be concluded. The parties to the complainant continue to explore other opportunities to set up an independent review and assessment mission to India.

case.title: POSCO Steel Project, Dhinkia and Gobindpur
case.place: Patana, Dhinkia panchayat, Jagatsinghpur district, Odisha, India
case.point: POSCO project area near Dhinkia (EJAtlas point, approximate)

lenders.name: POSCO (South Korea)
lenders.role: Signed a pact with the Odisha government in 2005 (22 May, per EJAtlas) for a planned US$12 billion, 12-million-tonne-a-year steel mill on 1,600 hectares (Reuters via Business Standard).

case.conditions: Foreign direct investment: the state committed to acquire land and help secure approvals for a South Korean steel company's plant (EJAtlas; Reuters via Business Standard).
case.community: On 2 March 2013 a bomb blast in Patana village killed three men opposed to the project, Tarun Mandal, Narahari Sahu and Manas Jena, and injured a fourth, Laxman Pramanik (fact-finding team, via Countercurrents). Police said they were probably making the bombs themselves; the protest group said project supporters attacked them (Reuters via Business Standard). A June 2008 bomb blast killed activist Tapan Mandal, Tarun's brother (fact-finding team). From early February 2013 at least 105 betel vine farms in Gobindpur were destroyed during land acquisition, and a 7 March 2013 police baton charge injured 41 villagers, including 35 women and children (fact-finding team). EJAtlas says the project threatened to displace over 22,000 people.
case.suppression: Twelve platoons of police were deployed in Gobindpur from 3 February 2013; police took more than 15 hours to reach the blast site and refused to register a complaint from a dead man's relative (fact-finding team, via Countercurrents). EJAtlas reports charges pending against more than 200 villagers in 2015.
case.outcome: Land acquisition resumed under heavy police presence the day after the 2013 deaths (Reuters via Business Standard). The state acquired 2,700 acres from 2012 to 2015; in April 2016 POSCO said the project was over (EJAtlas).
case.killed_note: Three killed in the March 2013 blast (Reuters; fact-finding team) and one activist killed in a 2008 blast (fact-finding team). A pro-POSCO man killed in a December 2011 blast is not counted.

complaint.title: Human Rights Law Centre and Raid vs G4S
complaint.subtitle: G4S’s contribution to human rights abuses of asylum seekers
affected: Other NCP's where the complaint was filed
complaint.allegations:
The complaint, submitted to both the UK and Australian NCPs, alleges that UK security contractor G4S failed to meet international standards and committed serious human rights violations in relation to the treatment of asylum seekers detained at an off-shore processing centre in Papua New Guinea (PNG).
The Australian Government established the centre in 2001 as an offshore processing centre. By agreement with PNG, asylum seekers arriving in Australia are forcibly transferred to Manus Island where they are mandatorily detained pending consideration of their refugee status. G4S was contracted by the Australian government to oversee management and security at the Manus Island Centre between February 2013 and March 2014.
Over this period, the Centre was repeatedly criticised by human rights organisations including the office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees for breaching basic minimum standards of care. The most serious incident occurred on 16-17 February 2014 when outbreaks of violence at the facility resulted in the death of an Iranian asylum seeker and injuries to up to 69 others. The outbreak of violence (in which G4S personnel were directly involved) is the subject of an on-going inquiry by the Australian Senate. Prior to the February violence, a number of other incidents had already raised concerns about detainee safety, such as physical violence, threats or aggression towards detainees by G4S personnel and sexual assaults.
The complainants propose the following recommendations to bring G4Ss policies and procedures in line with the OECD Guidelines: commitments with respect to a human rights framework for any future contracts it may enter into, commitments with respect to the payment of financial compensation to the detainees injured by G4S guards and to the family of the Iranian asylum seeker, disclosure of information on the outcomes of any internal investigations and disciplinary actions taken against staff involved in the violence, and disclosure of key documents which the company has not provided to the Senate Inquiry.
complaint.outcome:
In June 2015, the Australian NCP rejected the complaint citing three grounds. First of all, the NCP felt that aspects of the complaint could be interpreted as commentary on government policy. The NCP argued that G4S as service provider is not accountable for government policy and that other mechanisms exist for review and scrutiny of policy. Furthermore, the NCP did not consider it necessary to have a review of the conduct of G4S staff, as it would be unlikely to add further value to already existing reviews. Finally, the NCP claimed there were various legal proceedings in relation to incidents at the MRPC in which the NCP did not want to intervene.
The complainants did not feel that any of these three reasons provided valid grounds for rejecting the complaint, and they believe that the NCP violated the Procedural Guidance of the OECD Guidelines by rejecting the case based on criteria not stipulated in the Procedural Guidance.
On 2 July 2015, the complainants appealed the ANCP’s final assessment of the case. The ANCP reviewed the decision and decided to uphold its original decision. They provided their 2016 ANCP Response to the appeal as an appendix to its 27 October 2017 Appeal Statement. The appeal statement by the ANCP summarizes the case and the appeal process and then formally concludes the process with this statement “The ANCP acknowledges that at the time it was conducted, this appeal was not handled in line with published procedural guidance. The treasury is committed to improving the performance of the ANCP function. The 2017 independent review of the ANCP has been an important mechanism to assess the effectiveness of the ANCP’s structure and procedures, and will provide a further basis for considering improvements going forward.”
On 27 November, 2017, OECD Watch submits a substantiated submission to the OECD’s Investment Committee regarding the ANCP’s handling of this case.

cmp_record.t: G4S’s contribution to human rights abuses of asylum seekers

case.title: Manus detention centre: Reza Barati killed under G4S security
case.place: Manus Island Regional Processing Centre, Papua New Guinea
case.point: Lombrum Naval Base, Manus; the centre was on the base at Lombrum

lenders.name: Government of Australia
lenders.role: Paid for the offshore centre; G4S's contract was worth about A$244 million (RAID).

lenders.name: G4S (United Kingdom)
lenders.role: G4S Australia, wholly owned by G4S plc, ran management and security from October 2012 to March 2014 (RAID).

case.conditions: An outside government's money and a foreign company, not a loan. Australia held asylum seekers in Papua New Guinea under a private contract.
case.community: Three days of rioting in February 2014 during severe overcrowding left Iranian asylum seeker Reza Barati, 23, dead and at least 69 injured (RAID; SBS); the Cornall review counted 62 injured (The Conversation). Physical security arrangements were lacking, and detainees got little information on their claims (The Conversation).
case.suppression: A PNG police spokesman said in preliminary findings that local G4S guards carried out the suppression (Fairfax, Area News). The Cornall review found unclear roles between G4S and PNG police and recommended that the successor firm Transfield dismiss anyone implicated in assaults (The Conversation).
case.outcome: RAID and the Human Rights Law Centre complained under the OECD Guidelines in September 2014; Australia's contact point rejected it as commentary on government policy. A class action for 1,900 detainees was filed in December 2016 against Australia, G4S and Transfield (RAID).
case.killed_note: Barati was killed on 17 February 2014. Papua New Guinea's National Court convicted Louie Efi, employed by Loda Security and subcontracted to G4S, who dropped a large stone on him, and Joshua Kaluvia, a Salvation Army worker, who struck him with timber. Both were sentenced on 19 April 2016 to 10 years, five suspended. The court said expatriate and national G4S guards also kicked him. Counted because the man who struck the final blow was a guard working for G4S.

case.title: Renace Hydroelectric Complex on the Cahabón River, Built by Spain's Grupo Cobra
case.place: Cahabón river, San Pedro Carchá and Santa María Cahabón, Alta Verapaz, Guatemala
case.point: Renace complex on the Cahabón river (EJAtlas coordinates)

lenders.name: Grupo Cobra / ACS (Spain), builder of Renace from its second phase (foreign company)
lenders.role: Corporación Multi-Inversiones, the Guatemalan owner, contracted Cobra, a company of Florentino Pérez's ACS group, under a confidentiality agreement to build Renace from its second phase (eldiario.es; Alianza por la Solidaridad).

case.conditions: The sources name no outside lender behind the dams; the outside money was the foreign company's own. The developer is Renace, owned by Guatemala's Corporación Multi-Inversiones, which holds a 50-year concession on the river, with Cobra as contractor (eldiario.es).
case.community: The Renace complex has left about 30 km of the Cahabón river with little or no water in places, affecting about 29,000 Q'eqchi' people for whom the river is sacred, according to Alianza por la Solidaridad, whose findings and community interviews were reported by eldiario.es; of 50 affected communities only two have drinking water, a resident said (eldiario.es). Alianza found no environmental impact study for the first phase and said consultations for later phases surveyed 57 people (eldiario.es). In September 2015 the Environment Ministry fined the developer for failing environmental commitments for Renace II; communities reported intimidation, unpaid land payments and entry onto family land without permission from 2013 (EJAtlas).
case.suppression: People who object report being criminalised (eldiario.es).
case.outcome: Cobra says it bears no responsibility as a contractor hired by a Guatemalan company (eldiario.es). Q'eqchi' leader Bernardo Caal Xol, who denounced irregularities in licences for hydro projects such as the neighbouring Oxec dams, was detained on 30 January 2018 on charges brought by workers of an Oxec contractor and sentenced in November 2018 to more than 7 years; Amnesty International declared him a prisoner of conscience, and he was released in March 2022 (Alianza por la Solidaridad; Wikipedia).

complaint.title: ActionAid Italy et al. vs. JTF Tozzi Green
complaint.subtitle: Italian renewable energy company JTF Tozzy Green’s human rights impacts in Madagascar
complainants: Collective for the defense of Malagasy lands BMTT
complaint.allegations:
On 13 October 2023, ActionAid Italy, the collective for the defense of Malagasy lands BMTT, and Colletif Tany, filed a complaint at the Italian NCP against the Italian renewable energy company JTF Tozzi Green. The complainants allege that the leases and usage of land in Madagascar by JTF Tozzy Green’s subsidiary JTF Madagascar infringe on the human rights of the people living in the Ihorombe region.
According to the complainants, the agro-industrial activities of JTF Tozzy Green’s subsidiary contribute to worsening food security since its plantations use a lot of land and water, which have previously been used by the local population to grow their own food. They also say that the use of pesticides by JTF Tozzy Green’s subsidiary poses a risk to the health of people and the ecosystem. The complainants accuse JTF Tozzy Green of failure to adequately consult the people from the Ihorombe region before starting their plantations. Additionally, JTF Tozzy Green allegedly imposes penalties on local farmers for entering the land that was prior to JTF Tozzy Green’s lease of the land used by them for grazing their cattle. The complainants also claim that the company threatens the local population with charges of theft if they harvest seeds, used to plant JTF Tozzy Green’s corn, that have fallen to the ground.
All of the above leads the complainants to accuse JTF Tozzy Green of failures to comply with the standards in the Human Rights chapter of the OECD Guidelines, including failing to comply with Malagasy standards on free, prior, and informed consent of local communities and failing to provide transparency, appropriate information, and adequate participation before and during project implementation, resulting in social tensions, unmet expectations and unfair treatment.
The complainants are seeking JTF Tozzy Green to cease its operations and leave the Ihorombe region, and to return the monopolized land to local communities through a transparent, effective and participatory process. The complainants also demand compensation payments from JTF Tozzy Green to members of the affected peoples whose lands were occupied and seized, and that these sums be used to promote community projects.

cmp_record.pt: Ihosy, main town of Ihorombe region; plantation sites not given

case.title: Tozzi Green's Plantations on Ihorombe Grazing Land

lenders.name: Tozzi Green (Italy), through Jatropha Technology Farm Madagascar (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Has operated in Ihorombe since 2012 under two state land leases signed in 2012 and 2018 for 30 years at $65,600 a year (New Lines Magazine).

lenders.name: BIO (Belgian Investment Company for Developing Countries) and Finnfund (Finland)
lenders.role: State-owned development financiers. BIO granted a EUR 2.9 million loan to Tozzi Green's subsidiary JTF Madagascar in November 2019, part of a EUR 7.5 million combined investment with Finnfund announced in January 2020 (BIO).

case.conditions: The land was leased by the state; Satrokala villagers ceded about 600 acres around 2013, and Ivaro West residents gave community land free expecting benefits (New Lines Magazine).
case.community: The company grew jatropha, then maize, legumes and geraniums, and has planted about 14 square miles of trees for carbon credits, planned to reach almost 20 square miles by 2029 (New Lines Magazine). Herders have been fined or chased away with dogs when their zebu cattle strayed onto company land, and fear losing the grazing land altogether (New Lines Magazine).
case.suppression: In 2020 activist 'Maherelio' was arrested in Ihosy and released ten days later after protests; he was later convicted of extortion and abuse of office, which he denies (New Lines Magazine). In a May 2024 open letter Collectif Tany cited 'continuous pressure' and gendarmerie interventions (New Lines Magazine).
case.outcome: On 13 October 2023 ActionAid, BIMTT and Collectif Tany complained to Italy's OECD National Contact Point, alleging land dispossession and poor consultation and asking that the land be returned; more than a year later the parties had heard nothing from the contact point (New Lines Magazine). Tozzi Green says it acquired all land lawfully, calls the repression claims defamatory, and says gendarmes at meetings kept the atmosphere calm (New Lines Magazine).

complaint.allegations:
On 10 September 2024, the Indonesian community organisation ‘Caring Work Group on Work Strike in The Environment of PT Freeport Indonesia Papua – Timika – Jayapura – Jakarta’ filed a complaint against mining company Freeport-McMoRan Inc. (FCX) to the US NCP. The complaint focuses on FCX’s Indonesian subsidiary (PT Freeport Indonesia) and its links to workers’ and health rights harms. The complainant alleges that in 2017 over 3,000 Indonesian workers were dismissed from their employment for organising a strike permitted under Indonesian law, and that these dismissals have affected workers’ right to health due to lack of medical care. There is still no clarity on workers’ employment status and they have not received wages the complainant alleges is owed to them.
The complainants request for the NCP to offer its good offices to the parties to resolve the employment and other issues raised, including by fulfilling workers’ rights to wages and health insurance.

case.title: Grasberg Mine, Papua

lenders.name: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA)
lenders.role: In fiscal year 1990 guaranteed US$50 million of a US$500 million expansion of Freeport's copper, gold and silver mine in what was then Irian Jaya, covering breach of contract and war risks for 14 years. Freeport cancelled the MIGA cover in 1996 while MIGA was preparing to send an investigation team, per Down to Earth.

lenders.name: Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC, US government)
lenders.role: Cancelled a US$100 million political risk insurance policy in 1995 after a consultant's report found Freeport 'has devastated the river system'. Not part of the World Bank Group.

companies.name: Freeport-McMoRan
companies.role: Owner of the Grasberg mine and holder of the MIGA guarantee

case.community: Amungme people were displaced by the mine. In February 1995 about 2,000 people were ordered to leave the Waa, Tsinga and Arwaa valleys within three months, with no recorded consultation. Many displaced Indigenous people were moved to Kwamki-lama near Timika. In 1995 only 13% of Freeport's employees were Papuan.
case.suppression: The Australian Council for Overseas Aid (ACFOA) reported in April 1995 that at least 37 people, 22 of them civilians and 15 rebels, were killed or disappeared near the mine between June 1994 and February 1995, and that Freeport security staff joined the army in shootings, arrests and torture; houses were burned and gardens destroyed. Freeport and the Indonesian government denied the death figures. Villagers were also arrested, beaten and tortured.
case.ecosystem: In 1995 the mine released about 100,000 tonnes of waste rock slurry (tailings) a day into the Ajkwa River; a later NGO factsheet gives about 200,000 tonnes a day into three river systems. OPIC's consultant found 'excessive discharge and deposition of tailings'.
case.outcome: OPIC cancelled its insurance in 1995. Freeport dropped its MIGA cover in 1996 as MIGA prepared an investigation. Papuans sued Freeport in US courts over abuses by its security staff.
case.killed_note: ACFOA (April 1995): 37 killed by the Indonesian army June 1994 to February 1995, of them 22 civilians and 15 alleged guerrillas.
